Let's start with what's inside.
Every AI agent, regardless of type, is built from the same fundamental components.
There's the perception layer. This is how the agent receives information from the world around it.
At Solara, that might mean reading an incoming data feed from a solar installation,
receiving a user query, or picking up a trigger from a monitoring system.
There's the memory layer. As we covered in the last topic, agents hold short-term context
within a task and can access long-term memory from external storage.
This is what allows an agent to reason across multiple steps without losing track of where it is.
There's the reasoning engine, the LLM, which interprets what the agent has perceived,
decides what to do next, and determines which tools to use.
And there's the action layer. This is where the agent does something in the world,
runs a query, calls an API, writes a file, sends an alert.
These four components work together in a continuous loop.
The agent perceives, reasons, acts, then perceives again based on the result of that action.
That loop is what we call agent environment interaction.
And it's worth understanding because it's what separates an agent from a static tool.
A static tool waits to be asked. An agent operates within an environment.
It observes what's happening, decides what action is appropriate, and executes.
Then it checks the result, and decides what comes next.
At Solara, an agent monitoring grid performance isn't just waiting for someone to run a report.
It's watching. When output at a site drops below threshold, it observes the deviation,
decides the appropriate response, which might be querying historical data,
cross-referencing weather records, or escalating to a human operator, and takes that action.
The environment shapes the agent. The agent shapes the environment.
That bi-directional relationship is what makes agents useful in dynamic real-world data contexts.

because not every problem needs the same architecture. The first type is the reactive agent.
A reactive agent responds to its current input using predefined rules.
It has no memory of what happened before. No ability to plan ahead.
It simply observes the condition and responds. Think of a simple alert agent as Solara.
If output at Site 12 drops below 8% of a baseline, send an notification. That's a reactive agent.
Fast, predictable, easy to build, but limited. It can't investigate why the drop happened,
or determine whether the alert is actually worth sending. The second type is the goal-based agent.
A goal-based agent reasons about actions in terms of whether they move it closer to a defined
outcome. It plans and evaluates options. It chooses the path most likely to achieve the goal.
Solara's Site Performance Investigation Agent works this way. Its goal is to determine why Site 47
under-performed last Tuesday. It doesn't follow a fixed script. It decides what data to pull based on
what it finds, adjusting its approach as results come in. The third type is the utility-based agent.
A utility-based agent goes further than goal-based reasoning. It doesn't just ask,
will this action achieve the goal? It asks, which available action achieves the goal most
efficiently, at the lowest cost, and with the highest confidence. At Solara, a utility-based agent
managing report generation across hundreds of sites needs to make trade-off decisions constantly.
Do I generate a full diagnostic report or a summary? Do I escalate the anomaly or log it for review?
It evaluates options against a utility function and picks the best one. Let's zoom out and look at how
